From FreeMe to Ugly

By: Graham Coetzer | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We investigate allegations that one of SA's biggest wildlife rehabilitation centers shut it doors after the woman who was put in charge to run it, Margo Bansda, ran it into the ground.

Unique Selling Point:
Not only did the FreeMe Wildlife Rehab shut its doors months after Bansda took over amid a cloud of allegations of animal neglect and mismanagement, Bansda has kept it registered as a Non-Profit and still receives donations and bequests totaling hundreds of thousands of rands, which she seems to be using for her own benefit.

Summary:
By 2014 FreeMe was occupying land and buildings on the Rietfontein Reserve comprising of a house and outbuildings, covering 2 acres of land , by permission of City Parks, City of Johannesburg. There was NO LEASE in place.

FreeMe’s affairs were managed by a volunteer board of directors. It was the boards responsibility to properly administer all of the assets of FreeMe, and to carry out all of the obligations of FreeMe.

By the end of 2014, FreeMe:

…had 152 active volunteers, 26 of whom were members.

…had a contact list of some 800 individuals and organizations who supplied ancillary and other inputs to FreeMe.

… had acquired Nietgedacht Farm situate on Portion 1 of ERF 535 Randburg. This was funded for by donations from members of the public.

…admitted approximatly 900 new cases every month.

… had a permit issued by Gauteng Department of Agriculture and Rural Development (GDARD) authorising these activities.

…was accredited by the NSPCA.

… had an excellent continuous and regular inflow of funds from donations from generous members of the public. These were used to fund its activities. Funding was coming from small individual donations at fundraising drives, debit orders and large amounts received from corporate donors and bequests, all which had been built up over many years.


In 2015 Ms Margo Bansda was appointed as a paid management consultant by FreeMe and thereafter, on 1st March 2015, was appointed as a director of FreeMe. Ms Bansda then spoke of “restructuring” and issued accompanying emails and memoranda. A ‘new’ organization was presented to volunteers.

Board members resigned, and Ms Bansda appointed her friends as new board members.



All educational programmes, community outreach and orientation courses for new volunteers were terminated by Ms Bansda.

Over 50 charges of animal cruelty were laid against the Board of FreeMe at the NSPCA.



Further information:
In November 2015 the FreeMe operational permits became null and void. FreeMe was requested by GDARD to reapply for Operational permits. To this date no operational permits have been re-granted to FreeMe.

In December 2015 highly experienced Animal Manager Claudius Sibanda, key FreeMe employee of 12 years, was forced out of his employ and all attempts to receive his overtime pay and retrenchment package were blocked by the FreeMe directors. He never received a cent of severance.

Due to the closure of FreeMe, there was a crisis as there was suddenly nowhere for the public to take wildlife in need.

To fill this gap, FreeMe founder, ex director and ex CEO of FreeMe, Margi Brocklehurst formed a new Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre as a common law association, which was subsequently afforded NPO and PBO status. I was named “Friends of Free Wildlife (FFW)” in June 2016.

FFW rented premises in Kyalami, applied to GDARD for operational permits, and set out to rebuild a new centre as quickly as possible, with nothing but passion and great urgency.

FFW opened its doors to the public in July 2016, working under a permit of a fellow rehabilitation centre.

The FFW operational permits were granted in December 2016.

With the massive assistance from ex FreeMe volunteers and former FreeMe members, and the financial assistance of generous members of the public, so began the work to rebuild a new Wildlife Centre from scratch.

FreeMe was subsequently evicted from Rietfontein Reserve by Johannesburg City Parks in 2017.

The board of FreeMe liquidated all of its assets necessary to operate a wildlife centre in 2018.

Without operational permits and premises, FreeMe has been unable to carry out it functions and obligations as a Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre according to its MOI for the past 6 years.

FreeMe continues to accept donations and bequests from the unknowing public, even though it is non operational. Any donations to FreeMe (including bequests) are not finding their way to FFW which is doing the work the funds are intended to assist, and not being used to support the needs of urban wildlife at all.

FreeMe continues to maintain its registration with the Companies and Intellectual Properites Comission (CIPC). The company is registered to director Ms Bansda’s home address.

FreeMe was recently stripped of its Non- profit organization status by the Deprtment of Social Development.

FreeMe maintains its registration as a Public Benefit Organization (PBO) with SARS (TEU - Tax Exemption Unit) , even though it has not provided any “Benefit to the Public” in the past 6 years.

FreeMe has subsequently sold the land acquired with donor funds in 2010. (WOrth an estimated R2 million)

FreeMe maintains its existing contact details, unashamedly referring calls to Friends of Free Wildlife on a regular basis. They confirm to callers that FreeMe is temporarily closed and Friends of Free Wildlife will be able to assist.

FreeMe regularly and unashamedly refers calls to our FFW Pro Bono Veterinary Practice to assist with wildlife rescue and rehabilitation. FreeMe uses their contact details on their website as a point of refrence - without authorisation.

By 2022 FFW, under the guidance and leadership of its Board, has subsequently grown into a highly regarded rehabilitation centre with activities all over Gauteng.

Friends of Free Wildlife is managed by a volunteer board of directors coming from all walks of life, all passionate about wildlife.

FFW admit up to 400 new cases a month, depending on the time of the year.

Ex FreeMe volunteers, members and supporters have lodged hundreds of complaints with various authorities including SARS (TEU) since 8th December 2015 as well as the Companies and Intellectual Properties Comission (CIPC), notifying them of the closure of FreeMe. Investigations have been registered by these authorities, and clearly insufficient investigative steps have been taken.

The Department of Social Development (NPO) reciently launched an investigation into FreeMe which was immediatly stripped of its status as a Non Profit Organization.

In March 2016 Ms Rosemary Sims lodged a criminal charge at Sandton SAPS for fraud and theft of monies donated to FreeMe. The charge is laid against Ms Bansda, FreeMe Board members and Ms Pauline Walker.

Ms Sims’ charge was thereafter investigated. Ms Sims was interviewed by Investigating Officer Tina Meyer. There was a thorough investigation and a subpoena was issued in respect of FreeMe Financial Statements to undergo a SAPS Audit.


On 9th July 2018, Senior Public Prosecutor AM Smith of the National Prosecuting Authority sent a letter to Ms Sims. She indicated that FreeMe “was closed and not operating anymore” and there were no ‘books of account of this Centre’ and therefore they could not proceed with the investigation. This was incorrect as it appears the Investigating officer was misled in her investigations. The case was immediately reopened. It appears no further investigative steps have been taken by SAPS to date.

Members of the public have the right to be informed that FreeMe Wildlife NPC is no longer operational. They have the right to know what their donor funds are being spent on. They have the right to make the decision as to where they would like their donor funds and bequests to be redirected to or to be cancelled.

Script:


FREEME
Second Draft Script
15 March 2022


Voice
These buildings in the Rietfontein Nature Reserve in Johannesburg once held the FreeMe Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre - not to be mistaken for a similarly named organisation in KZN. And before it’s rather spectacular fall from grace, this woman, Margi Brocklehurst, poured her heart and soul into it.

Sound Up Margi
Derek: Margi, what’s it like coming back here?

Margi: This is tough hey. This is really, really not good for me.

Voice
This footage, from 2007, shows Margi and the FreeMe team doing what they did best, saving urban wildlife. The orphaned or injured animals that you might find in your garden or home. Today, the deserted buildings tell a different story…

Sound Up Margi
Margi: This is really, really, devastating to be here today.

Derek: Let’s not torture you any further.

Voice
This is what a working wildlife rehabilitation centre looks like. Friends of Free Wildlife is Margi’s new facility, started in 2016 to fill the void after the collapse of FreeMe. Veterinarian Dr Perushan Yenketsamy is just one of the people who offers his time and expertise here on a pro bono basis.

Sound Up Persushan
We see literally anything from a little Sparrow with an injured wing, to eagles, owls, small mammals, dassies.

Sound Up Margi Brocklehurst
Derek: Margi, you started out as a volunteer with the original FreeMe way back in 1997?

Margi: Yip, we started in one room, in a house on Rietfontein, and a few years later we’d taken over the entire building. So yes, it grew very quickly.

Voice
With her enviable skills in both saving wildlife and raising much needed funds, Margi soon became a director of the not for profit FreeMe. She says that during their heyday FreeMe was accredited by the NSPCA, had a 152 volunteers and took in an average of 800 patients every month.

Sound Up Margi
We had an exceptional reputation with vets and other people in the field.

Voice
With donations pouring in from a willing public, FreeMe was able to acquire this plot of land, which was supposed to become its permanent home.

Sound Up Margi
When I left FreeMe in 2010, I’d left them with nearly R2 million in the bank, that was fund raised by myself and the team.

Voice
Then, in 2015, FreeMe’s board appointed a new managing director. Her name? Margo Bansda. A self proclaimed international business strategist, visionary and mediator.

Link Derek
Some say that’s when the organisation went into a downward spiral.

Voice
Margi says despite her impressive cv, Margo Bansda had no prior experience working in wildlife rehabilitation.

Sound Up Margi
It was one person’s opinion of how a wildlife centre should be run, with no experience behind that opinion, which made life impossible at the centre at that time.

Voice
It seems not everyone at FreeMe agreed with Bansda’s attempts at restructuring the organisation, and after a disciplinary hearing of senior animal managers resulted in them resigning from FreeMe, many volunteers left as well.

Sound Up Margi
And because there was no one else to do it, it just failed dramatically.

Voice
But, there was a problem: FreeMe’s operating permit - issued by the Gauteng Government - was held in the name of one of the wildlife managers who decided to leave.

Sound Up Margi
They didn’t realise that these permits needed renewing in a new name.

Voice
No surprise then that, in 2015, just months after Margo took over the reigns the unthinkable happened: FreeMe was closed temporarily because it no longer had a valid permit.

Link Derek
By the middle of 2016 FreeMe had lost their permit, they were no longer allowed to keep or care for animals. They were officially closed.

Voice
The last of the animals were removed from the premises by April 2017. And images like these are a stark reminder of their dramatic downfall.

Sound Up Margi

Margi: I do believe Margo Bansda is responsible for bringing FreeMe to closure.

Voice
Margo Bansda declined our request for an on camera interview, but did say:

“…the application process needed proof of a lease to operate on land owned by City Parks.” That, she says, was never in place.

Despite the fact that FreeMe has not been operational in wildlife rehabilitation since at least 2017, it is still a registered Not For Profit Company, and it’s bank accounts remain open.

Sound Up Margi
Derek: Margi, some donations came in the form of monthly debit orders, made out to FreeMe, what happened to those?

Margi: Many of those debit orders are still going into the FreeMe bank account.

Sound Up Margi
Derek: Margi, some donations came in the form of monthly debit orders, made out to FreeMe, what happened to those?

Margi: Many of those debit orders are still going into the FreeMe bank account, and I know that because about 6 or 8 months ago I was giving a talk to one of the large bird clubs, and afterwards a lady came to me and she said for the last 6 years I’ve been putting a R100 a month into the FreeMe account, I never knew that it was closed.

Voice
In fact, leaked statements from some of FreeMe’s bank accounts for the period 2017 until 2021 show that FreeMe received R934 834 from members of the public in the form of donations and bequests, during a period that FreeMe was not operational as a rehabilitation centre.

Sound Up Margi
those people are literally being swindled out of that money.

Voice
Margo Bansda said all FreeMe funds were accounted for in their Audited Financial Statements. But she refused to provide us those, and said we’d need to apply to see them through a Promotion of Access to Information request. So we decided to phone her and ask why not?

Sound Up Margo
Derek: But you’re a non profit company, so why not just give us access so that we know what’s going on in this so called FreeMe?

Margo: Why can you just not actually go via the proper processes and request it?

Voice
While Carte Blanche is all for due process, we’re not keen on needless delays when public funds are at stake.

Sound Up Margo

Derek: Margo, it’s sounds like you’re more interested in following due process than saving wildlife?

Margo: But we have to…

Derek: Sad to say it.

Margo: But we can’t, we can’t do that right now. We cannot do that right now because we need a location and we’re in hibernation. We’re busy working out where do we go to, where do we get a permit. It’s a very expensive exercise to actually embark on.

Derek: It’s taken five years so far?

Margo: uhm…

Voice
The statements we’ve had sight of show payments with references to Margo Bansda totalling R314 606 for the same period.

Sound Up Margo
Derek: Payments with references to Margo Bansda as consulting fees or refunds totalled over R313 000?

Margo: No, you are joking.

Derek: I’m not joking, we’ve seen it.

Margo: You are joking. You are joking.

Derek: We’ve seen it Margo.

Margo: You need to know a lot more then that, which you actually don’t know.

Derek: About due process?

Margo: No, ja that too.

Derek: Those same statements show an income of R621 000 from bequests, and R313 000 from donations over the same period. That’s just under a million rand, meant for the rehab of wildlife, and it’s n to being done.

Margo: Derek, your figures are wrong.

Derek: Well it’s hard to argue with you if I can’t sit down and look at your statements. And you say we must go the long process, go the legal route, you’re an NPC, a non profit company, just show us your audited financial statements?

Margo: Derek, we’ve asked you to interview, we requested, we requested a full interview with you without cameras, so that we can actually give you the full expose’ on FreeMe. You have chosen, not to do that.

Derek: Margo, we are a television company, we don’t operate in private little meetings without cameras.

Voice
Margo said all her donors had been made aware of the current situation, and some of them continued to donate by free choice. But it didn’t take us long to find people like businessman Matthew Haifer, who did not know FreeMe was no longer operational.

Sound Up Matthew
Derek: Matthew you’ve been donating to FreeMe for sometime now?

Matthew: Correct ja, probably over ten years.

Derek: Did they ever tell you did it close down?

Matthew: No, no, I mean I had no idea.

Voice
And while Margo hasn’t run wildlife rehab for years, she’s been happy to refer animals in need to Dr Yenketsamy’s private practice, The Bryanston Avian, Exotic and Small animal’s clinic.

Sound Up Perushan
Our phone number for the practice is on the FreeMe website, which we have not given them permission for.

Sound Up Margo
Derek: Why does your website use Perushan’s Bryanston clinic telephone number under general enquiries?

Margo: It is not in general enquiries, it is emergencies because people actually do phone, and people do ask what can they do with specific animals.

Voice
But it was under General Enquiries, and it was only changed the day after our phone call.

And what about the land acquired by FreeMe more than 15 years ago? Well, it’s been for sale. But Margo says it currently remains an asset of FreeMe.


Friends of Free Wildlife meanwhile has offered to take over the running of FreeMe but Margi says the negotiations have only led to more mud slinging.

Sound Up Margo
Margo: So until a whole lot of matters are cleared up, then we will discuss other…

Derek: So until then you’ll continue taking donations and bequests…

Margo: No, we have not taken…

Derek: And it seems the big losers in this whole dilemma are the animals.

Voice
And perhaps that, more than anything else, is the real tragedy behind this story.


END






PROMO 1 (21sec)
Sound Up Birds

Voice
A popular wildlife sanctuary with an impeccable reputation.

Sound Up Margi
Describe success

Voice
So how was 18 years of hard work destroyed in a matter of months?

Sound Up Derek
That’s just under a million rand, meant for the rehab of wildlife, and it’s not being done.


Promo 2 (21sec)
Voice
For four years the donations kept pouring into the bank accounts of a well known wildlife centre.

Sound Up Margi
This is really, really not good for me.

Voice
But little did some donors know that the organisation had long since closed its doors

Sound Up

Voice
So what happened to all their money?

Promo 3 (11sec)

When human beings collide, wild animals are often the ultimate losers. A closer look at a wildlife NPC gone horribly wrong.

references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 20 March 2022 - Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 31 March 2022 Script: FREEME Second Draft Script 15 March 2022 Voice These buildings in the Rietfontein Nature Reserve in Johannesburg once held the FreeMe Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre - not to be mistaken for a similarly named organisation in KZN. And before it’s rather spectacular fall from grace, this woman, Margi Brocklehurst, poured her heart and soul into it. Sound Up Margi Derek: Margi, what’s it like coming back here? Margi: This is tough hey. This is really, really not good for me. Voice This footage, from 2007, shows Margi and the FreeMe team doing what they did best, saving urban wildlife. The orphaned or injured animals that you might find in your garden or home. Today, the deserted buildings tell a different story… Sound Up Margi Margi: This is really, really, devastating to be here today. Derek: Let’s not torture you any further. Voice This is what a working wildlife rehabilitation centre looks like. Friends of Free Wildlife is Margi’s new facility, started in 2016 to fill the void after the collapse of FreeMe. Veterinarian Dr Perushan Yenketsamy is just one of the people who offers his time and expertise here on a pro bono basis. Sound Up Persushan We see literally anything from a little Sparrow with an injured wing, to eagles, owls, small mammals, dassies. Sound Up Margi Brocklehurst Derek: Margi, you started out as a volunteer with the original FreeMe way back in 1997? Margi: Yip, we started in one room, in a house on Rietfontein, and a few years later we’d taken over the entire building. So yes, it grew very quickly. Voice With her enviable skills in both saving wildlife and raising much needed funds, Margi soon became a director of the not for profit FreeMe. She says that during their heyday FreeMe was accredited by the NSPCA, had a 152 volunteers and took in an average of 800 patients every month. Sound Up Margi We had an exceptional reputation with vets and other people in the field. Voice With donations pouring in from a willing public, FreeMe was able to acquire this plot of land, which was supposed to become its permanent home. Sound Up Margi When I left FreeMe in 2010, I’d left them with nearly R2 million in the bank, that was fund raised by myself and the team. Voice Then, in 2015, FreeMe’s board appointed a new managing director. Her name? Margo Bansda. A self proclaimed international business strategist, visionary and mediator. Link Derek Some say that’s when the organisation went into a downward spiral. Voice Margi says despite her impressive cv, Margo Bansda had no prior experience working in wildlife rehabilitation. Sound Up Margi It was one person’s opinion of how a wildlife centre should be run, with no experience behind that opinion, which made life impossible at the centre at that time. Voice It seems not everyone at FreeMe agreed with Bansda’s attempts at restructuring the organisation, and after a disciplinary hearing of senior animal managers resulted in them resigning from FreeMe, many volunteers left as well. Sound Up Margi And because there was no one else to do it, it just failed dramatically. Voice But, there was a problem: FreeMe’s operating permit - issued by the Gauteng Government - was held in the name of one of the wildlife managers who decided to leave. Sound Up Margi They didn’t realise that these permits needed renewing in a new name. Voice No surprise then that, in 2015, just months after Margo took over the reigns the unthinkable happened: FreeMe was closed temporarily because it no longer had a valid permit. Link Derek By the middle of 2016 FreeMe had lost their permit, they were no longer allowed to keep or care for animals. They were officially closed. Voice The last of the animals were removed from the premises by April 2017. And images like these are a stark reminder of their dramatic downfall. Sound Up Margi Margi: I do believe Margo Bansda is responsible for bringing FreeMe to closure. Voice Margo Bansda declined our request for an on camera interview, but did say: “…the application process needed proof of a lease to operate on land owned by City Parks.” That, she says, was never in place. Despite the fact that FreeMe has not been operational in wildlife rehabilitation since at least 2017, it is still a registered Not For Profit Company, and it’s bank accounts remain open. Sound Up Margi Derek: Margi, some donations came in the form of monthly debit orders, made out to FreeMe, what happened to those? Margi: Many of those debit orders are still going into the FreeMe bank account. Sound Up Margi Derek: Margi, some donations came in the form of monthly debit orders, made out to FreeMe, what happened to those? Margi: Many of those debit orders are still going into the FreeMe bank account, and I know that because about 6 or 8 months ago I was giving a talk to one of the large bird clubs, and afterwards a lady came to me and she said for the last 6 years I’ve been putting a R100 a month into the FreeMe account, I never knew that it was closed. Voice In fact, leaked statements from some of FreeMe’s bank accounts for the period 2017 until 2021 show that FreeMe received R934 834 from members of the public in the form of donations and bequests, during a period that FreeMe was not operational as a rehabilitation centre. Sound Up Margi those people are literally being swindled out of that money. Voice Margo Bansda said all FreeMe funds were accounted for in their Audited Financial Statements. But she refused to provide us those, and said we’d need to apply to see them through a Promotion of Access to Information request. So we decided to phone her and ask why not? Sound Up Margo Derek: But you’re a non profit company, so why not just give us access so that we know what’s going on in this so called FreeMe? Margo: Why can you just not actually go via the proper processes and request it? Voice While Carte Blanche is all for due process, we’re not keen on needless delays when public funds are at stake. Sound Up Margo Derek: Margo, it’s sounds like you’re more interested in following due process than saving wildlife? Margo: But we have to… Derek: Sad to say it. Margo: But we can’t, we can’t do that right now. We cannot do that right now because we need a location and we’re in hibernation. We’re busy working out where do we go to, where do we get a permit. It’s a very expensive exercise to actually embark on. Derek: It’s taken five years so far? Margo: uhm… Voice The statements we’ve had sight of show payments with references to Margo Bansda totalling R314 606 for the same period. Sound Up Margo Derek: Payments with references to Margo Bansda as consulting fees or refunds totalled over R313 000? Margo: No, you are joking. Derek: I’m not joking, we’ve seen it. Margo: You are joking. You are joking. Derek: We’ve seen it Margo. Margo: You need to know a lot more then that, which you actually don’t know. Derek: About due process? Margo: No, ja that too. Derek: Those same statements show an income of R621 000 from bequests, and R313 000 from donations over the same period. That’s just under a million rand, meant for the rehab of wildlife, and it’s n to being done. Margo: Derek, your figures are wrong. Derek: Well it’s hard to argue with you if I can’t sit down and look at your statements. And you say we must go the long process, go the legal route, you’re an NPC, a non profit company, just show us your audited financial statements? Margo: Derek, we’ve asked you to interview, we requested, we requested a full interview with you without cameras, so that we can actually give you the full expose’ on FreeMe. You have chosen, not to do that. Derek: Margo, we are a television company, we don’t operate in private little meetings without cameras. Voice Margo said all her donors had been made aware of the current situation, and some of them continued to donate by free choice. But it didn’t take us long to find people like businessman Matthew Haifer, who did not know FreeMe was no longer operational. Sound Up Matthew Derek: Matthew you’ve been donating to FreeMe for sometime now? Matthew: Correct ja, probably over ten years. Derek: Did they ever tell you did it close down? Matthew: No, no, I mean I had no idea. Voice And while Margo hasn’t run wildlife rehab for years, she’s been happy to refer animals in need to Dr Yenketsamy’s private practice, The Bryanston Avian, Exotic and Small animal’s clinic. Sound Up Perushan Our phone number for the practice is on the FreeMe website, which we have not given them permission for. Sound Up Margo Derek: Why does your website use Perushan’s Bryanston clinic telephone number under general enquiries? Margo: It is not in general enquiries, it is emergencies because people actually do phone, and people do ask what can they do with specific animals. Voice But it was under General Enquiries, and it was only changed the day after our phone call. And what about the land acquired by FreeMe more than 15 years ago? Well, it’s been for sale. But Margo says it currently remains an asset of FreeMe. Friends of Free Wildlife meanwhile has offered to take over the running of FreeMe but Margi says the negotiations have only led to more mud slinging. Sound Up Margo Margo: So until a whole lot of matters are cleared up, then we will discuss other… Derek: So until then you’ll continue taking donations and bequests… Margo: No, we have not taken… Derek: And it seems the big losers in this whole dilemma are the animals. Voice And perhaps that, more than anything else, is the real tragedy behind this story. END PROMO 1 (21sec) Sound Up Birds Voice A popular wildlife sanctuary with an impeccable reputation. Sound Up Margi Describe success Voice So how was 18 years of hard work destroyed in a matter of months? Sound Up Derek That’s just under a million rand, meant for the rehab of wildlife, and it’s not being done. Promo 2 (21sec) Voice For four years the donations kept pouring into the bank accounts of a well known wildlife centre. Sound Up Margi This is really, really not good for me. Voice But little did some donors know that the organisation had long since closed its doors Sound Up Voice So what happened to all their money? Promo 3 (11sec) When human beings collide, wild animals are often the ultimate losers. A closer look at a wildlife NPC gone horribly wrong.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We investigate allegations that one of SA's biggest wildlife rehabilitation centers shut it doors after the woman who was put in charge to run it, Margo Bansda, ran it into the ground.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Not only did the FreeMe Wildlife Rehab shut its doors months after Bansda took over amid a cloud of allegations of animal neglect and mismanagement, Bansda has kept it registered as a Non-Profit and still receives donations and bequests totaling hundreds of thousands of rands, which she seems to be using for her own benefit.
metadata.Summary: By 2014 FreeMe was occupying land and buildings on the Rietfontein Reserve comprising of a house and outbuildings, covering 2 acres of land , by permission of City Parks, City of Johannesburg. There was NO LEASE in place. FreeMe’s affairs were managed by a volunteer board of directors. It was the boards responsibility to properly administer all of the assets of FreeMe, and to carry out all of the obligations of FreeMe. By the end of 2014, FreeMe: …had 152 active volunteers, 26 of whom were members. …had a contact list of some 800 individuals and organizations who supplied ancillary and other inputs to FreeMe. … had acquired Nietgedacht Farm situate on Portion 1 of ERF 535 Randburg. This was funded for by donations from members of the public. …admitted approximatly 900 new cases every month. … had a permit issued by Gauteng Department of Agriculture and Rural Development (GDARD) authorising these activities. …was accredited by the NSPCA. … had an excellent continuous and regular inflow of funds from donations from generous members of the public. These were used to fund its activities. Funding was coming from small individual donations at fundraising drives, debit orders and large amounts received from corporate donors and bequests, all which had been built up over many years. In 2015 Ms Margo Bansda was appointed as a paid management consultant by FreeMe and thereafter, on 1st March 2015, was appointed as a director of FreeMe. Ms Bansda then spoke of “restructuring” and issued accompanying emails and memoranda. A ‘new’ organization was presented to volunteers. Board members resigned, and Ms Bansda appointed her friends as new board members. All educational programmes, community outreach and orientation courses for new volunteers were terminated by Ms Bansda. Over 50 charges of animal cruelty were laid against the Board of FreeMe at the NSPCA.
metadata.Further information: In November 2015 the FreeMe operational permits became null and void. FreeMe was requested by GDARD to reapply for Operational permits. To this date no operational permits have been re-granted to FreeMe. In December 2015 highly experienced Animal Manager Claudius Sibanda, key FreeMe employee of 12 years, was forced out of his employ and all attempts to receive his overtime pay and retrenchment package were blocked by the FreeMe directors. He never received a cent of severance. Due to the closure of FreeMe, there was a crisis as there was suddenly nowhere for the public to take wildlife in need. To fill this gap, FreeMe founder, ex director and ex CEO of FreeMe, Margi Brocklehurst formed a new Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre as a common law association, which was subsequently afforded NPO and PBO status. I was named “Friends of Free Wildlife (FFW)” in June 2016. FFW rented premises in Kyalami, applied to GDARD for operational permits, and set out to rebuild a new centre as quickly as possible, with nothing but passion and great urgency. FFW opened its doors to the public in July 2016, working under a permit of a fellow rehabilitation centre. The FFW operational permits were granted in December 2016. With the massive assistance from ex FreeMe volunteers and former FreeMe members, and the financial assistance of generous members of the public, so began the work to rebuild a new Wildlife Centre from scratch. FreeMe was subsequently evicted from Rietfontein Reserve by Johannesburg City Parks in 2017. The board of FreeMe liquidated all of its assets necessary to operate a wildlife centre in 2018. Without operational permits and premises, FreeMe has been unable to carry out it functions and obligations as a Wildlife Rehabilitation Centre according to its MOI for the past 6 years. FreeMe continues to accept donations and bequests from the unknowing public, even though it is non operational. Any donations to FreeMe (including bequests) are not finding their way to FFW which is doing the work the funds are intended to assist, and not being used to support the needs of urban wildlife at all. FreeMe continues to maintain its registration with the Companies and Intellectual Properites Comission (CIPC). The company is registered to director Ms Bansda’s home address. FreeMe was recently stripped of its Non- profit organization status by the Deprtment of Social Development. FreeMe maintains its registration as a Public Benefit Organization (PBO) with SARS (TEU - Tax Exemption Unit) , even though it has not provided any “Benefit to the Public” in the past 6 years. FreeMe has subsequently sold the land acquired with donor funds in 2010. (WOrth an estimated R2 million) FreeMe maintains its existing contact details, unashamedly referring calls to Friends of Free Wildlife on a regular basis. They confirm to callers that FreeMe is temporarily closed and Friends of Free Wildlife will be able to assist. FreeMe regularly and unashamedly refers calls to our FFW Pro Bono Veterinary Practice to assist with wildlife rescue and rehabilitation. FreeMe uses their contact details on their website as a point of refrence - without authorisation. By 2022 FFW, under the guidance and leadership of its Board, has subsequently grown into a highly regarded rehabilitation centre with activities all over Gauteng. Friends of Free Wildlife is managed by a volunteer board of directors coming from all walks of life, all passionate about wildlife. FFW admit up to 400 new cases a month, depending on the time of the year. Ex FreeMe volunteers, members and supporters have lodged hundreds of complaints with various authorities including SARS (TEU) since 8th December 2015 as well as the Companies and Intellectual Properties Comission (CIPC), notifying them of the closure of FreeMe. Investigations have been registered by these authorities, and clearly insufficient investigative steps have been taken. The Department of Social Development (NPO) reciently launched an investigation into FreeMe which was immediatly stripped of its status as a Non Profit Organization. In March 2016 Ms Rosemary Sims lodged a criminal charge at Sandton SAPS for fraud and theft of monies donated to FreeMe. The charge is laid against Ms Bansda, FreeMe Board members and Ms Pauline Walker. Ms Sims’ charge was thereafter investigated. Ms Sims was interviewed by Investigating Officer Tina Meyer. There was a thorough investigation and a subpoena was issued in respect of FreeMe Financial Statements to undergo a SAPS Audit. On 9th July 2018, Senior Public Prosecutor AM Smith of the National Prosecuting Authority sent a letter to Ms Sims. She indicated that FreeMe “was closed and not operating anymore” and there were no ‘books of account of this Centre’ and therefore they could not proceed with the investigation. This was incorrect as it appears the Investigating officer was misled in her investigations. The case was immediately reopened. It appears no further investigative steps have been taken by SAPS to date. Members of the public have the right to be informed that FreeMe Wildlife NPC is no longer operational. They have the right to know what their donor funds are being spent on. They have the right to make the decision as to where they would like their donor funds and bequests to be redirected to or to be cancelled.
